title: Bernie Sanders: Winning the Midterms Is Not Enough. Here’s What We Must Do
content:
The American people understand that the economy today is rigged and that we cannot continue the ‘same old, same old’ establishment politics and establishment policies.




 




Bernie Sanders




Nov 05, 2026




Common Dreams




 




On Tuesday, Trump told us to vote as if he were on the ballot. And that is exactly what the American people did.




 




Together, we stood up to 

authoritarianism

 and a president who does not believe in the Constitution or the 

rule of law

. And we won.




 




With Democratic control over the Senate and the House, we will now—finally—be able to hold 

Donald Trump

 accountable.




 




The American people have had enough. They are demanding real change and bold policies that will dramatically improve their lives.




 




That is a big deal. But as important as it is, it is not enough. We have got to do more.




 




Whether we like it or not, we are living in an unprecedented moment in American history where our country faces extraordinary crises. We cannot and must not run away from them when Democrats assume power in January.




 




These crises must be dealt with.




 




It is no secret that in the 

United States

 and all over the world, people are giving up on 

democracy

. Now, why is that?




 




And the answer is that—all over the world, not just in America—working families are struggling to put food on the table and pay for basic necessities while the very richest people become much richer. And, throughout our country and in many other countries, ordinary people are saying, ‘Does their government even know that they exist?’ Or are elected officials too busy worrying about the needs of the rich and the powerful?




 




This is an American issue, but, in fact, an international issue.




 




And in my view, the American people have had enough. They are demanding real change and bold policies that will dramatically improve their lives.




 




In the richest country on Earth, the American people want a government that stands for working families, not billionaire campaign contributors. And that is not just 

Bernie Sanders

 talking.




 




According to a recent AP poll, 80% of registered voters want either “complete and total upheaval” or “substantial change” in how this country is run. And that includes 97% of Democrats, 90% of independents, and 58% of 

Republicans

.




 




In other words, the American people understand that the economy today is rigged and that we cannot continue the ‘same old, same old’ establishment politics and establishment policies.




 




The American people want change. Real change. And the midterm election confirms just that.




 




Let me give you some examples of what I mean and the issues that we have got to deal with.




 




In our country today, income and 

wealth inequality

 has reached unprecedented levels. The top 1% now owns more wealth than the bottom 93%. One man, 

Elon Musk

, owns more wealth than the bottom 53% of American households. In my view, that is insane. And I think that’s how most Americans feel.




 




Democrats, when they gain control, in January, of the House and the Senate, cannot ignore this grotesque 

inequality

. We must take on the greed of the very, very rich and their incredible wealth.




 




We must enact a 5% wealth tax on billionaires so that we can provide every working-class family in the country, a family of four, with a $12,000 direct payment.




 




And that means a Democratic Congress must pass a wealth tax on billionaires.




 




At a time when billionaires pay a lower effective tax rate than truck drivers or nurses, we must enact a 5% wealth tax on billionaires so that we can provide every working-class family in the country, a family of four, with a $12,000 direct payment. In other words, if you’re a working-class family of four, that’s $3,000 for every man, woman, and child—$12,000.




 




Furthermore, with that tax on billionaires, we can build 7 million units of low-income and 

affordable housing

, we can make public colleges and universities tuition-free, and we can provide universal free child care for 13 million 

children

. That is what a wealth tax on billionaires can do.




 




But taxing the oligarchs means more than just taking on their wealth. 

It means ending their stranglehold over our political system.




 




Elon Musk

 and his billionaire friends have poured a record-breaking $2 billion into the recent election. That is absurd.




 




The American people want Congress to overturn 

Citizens United

, abolish 

super PACs

, and establish public funding of elections. Democracy must mean one person, one vote, not billionaires buying elections.




 




But it’s not just massive income and wealth inequality that we have to deal with or a corrupt 

campaign finance

 system.




 




In America today—as everybody knows, and I get the same response wherever I go in this country—everybody understands that our 

healthcare

 system is broken. It is dysfunctional. And it is wildly expensive.




 




We spend almost twice as much per person on healthcare as any other major country. Yet, despite that huge expenditure, more than 90 million Americans are uninsured or underinsured. Over half a million people go bankrupt each year because of medical debt. We pay the highest prescription 

drug prices

 in the world. And tragically, more than 60,000 Americans die unnecessarily every year because they cannot afford medical care.




 




How cruel is that?




 




Yes, we must repeal the $1 trillion in cuts Trump made to 

Medicaid

 and the 

Affordable Care Act

 to prevent 15 million Americans from losing their healthcare. Yes, we must restore ACA tax credits to stop the outrageous premium spikes for 20 million Americans, but that is nowhere near enough. Healthcare must be considered as a human right, not a privilege. That means passing 

Medicare for all

 legislation now supported by 66% of the American people.




 




As an immediate first step, Democrats must lower the 

Medicare

 eligibility age from 65 down to 55, expand Medicare to cover dental, vision, and hearing, and guarantee universal healthcare coverage for every child from birth through age 19. All of this can be accomplished with 51 votes in the Senate, through the reconciliation process.




 




But it’s not just income and wealth inequality that we have to deal with, or a corrupt campaign finance system or a dysfunctional healthcare system. We must deal with artificial intelligence—the most transformational 

technology

 in the history of humanity.




 




In America today, 

big tech

 oligarchs are spending trillions of dollars on 

artificial intelligence

 and robotics with virtually no regulation.




 




Democrats must enact a national moratorium on AI data centers, must pause advanced AI development and ban superintelligence.




 




This revolutionary technology will transform the lives of every man, woman, and child in our country and around the world. Left unchecked, AI and robotics will destroy tens of millions of jobs, devastate our children’s mental health, eviscerate our 

privacy

 rights, drive up electricity rates, strain 

water

 supplies, and transform warfare.




 




If AI becomes smarter than human beings and escapes human control, it will also pose an existential threat to the very existence of humanity. We cannot allow a handful of big tech billionaires to become even richer and more powerful by ramming this dangerous technology down our throats.




 




Democrats must enact a national moratorium on AI data centers, must pause advanced AI development and ban superintelligence.




 




And by the way, I might mention that in the election, in dozens of communities throughout our country, citizens voted for a moratorium on the construction of data centers. In other words, a moratorium on data centers is exactly what the American people want.




 




But my friends, it is not just 

oligarchy

, a corrupt campaign finance system, a broken healthcare system, and uncontrolled AI.




 




In America today, while the very rich get richer, 60% of our people live paycheck to paycheck and millions work long, long hours for incredibly low wages. That must change.




 




A job must lift people out of 

poverty

, not keep them in it.




 




The $7.25-an-hour federal 

minimum wage

 is a 

starvation

 wage. Democrats must raise it to a living wage of at least $20-an-hour and make it easier for 

workers

 to form 

unions

 by passing the PRO Act. A job must lift people out of poverty, not keep them in it.




 




Further, in our country today, one-third of our seniors are struggling economically, and more than 20% are trying to survive on less than $15,000 a year. Nearly half of older Americans have no retirement savings and no idea how they will retire with a shred of dignity. Meanwhile, Elon Musk pays the same amount into 

Social Security

 as someone earning $184,600 a year. That is absurd.




 




By applying the Social Security payroll tax to all income above $250,000, including capital gains and dividends, we could increase benefits by $2,400 a year, lift millions of seniors out of poverty, improve cost of living adjustments, and keep Social Security solvent for generations without raising taxes on the bottom 91% of Americans.




 




We must also restore the traditional pension plans corporate America took away so that every worker can count on a guaranteed income in retirement.




 




That is what a Democratic Congress must do.




 




Let me be clear. In America today, we spend more on the military than the next six nations combined. Despite massive waste, fraud, and abuse, the 

Pentagon

 has repeatedly failed independent audits and cannot account for trillions of dollars in spending. Adding insult to injury, Trump has dragged us into an illegal and unconstitutional war in Iran that will cost hundreds of billions of dollars.




 




We must end this disastrous war.




 




We must cut off all funding for the genocidal government in Israel.




 




And we must substantially reduce 

military spending

.




 




Instead of pouring $1.1 trillion into a bloated Pentagon and never-ending wars, a Democratic Congress must build the best public education system in the world with no teacher earning less than $60,000 a year.




 




We are fighting to give hope to the American people—to allow them to understand that their government can work for them, can address the crises that they face, and will pay attention to the needs of the men, women and children in our country who are struggling, and not just the very, very wealthy campaign contributors.




 




And let me touch on one more subject that Democrats must deal with.




 




Since Trump took office, ICE agents have shot American citizens in cold blood, have broken down doors to arrest people, and have sent five-year-old children to detention centers. These actions are not only immoral and disgraceful, they are unconstitutional.




 




Democrats must immediately rein in the $75 billion Republicans gave Trump to fund his domestic army. Instead of ICE agents terrorizing communities throughout the country, we must finally move to comprehensive 

immigration

 reform and a path toward citizenship for the undocumented.




 




Let’s be clear: All of the policies I have just discussed—and more that I have not mentioned—are not radical.




 




They are precisely what a strong majority of the American people want.




 




So we are in a moment in American history where a lot of folks are losing faith in democracy. They are struggling every day just to stay alive while, at the same time, billionaires have more money than they can spend in a thousand lifetimes and are getting richer and richer all of the time.




 




What we are talking about now is not only the need to fight for economic justice.




 




We are fighting to give hope to the American people—to allow them to understand that their government can work for them, can address the crises that they face, and will pay attention to the needs of the men, women and children in our country who are struggling, and not just the very, very wealthy campaign contributors.




 




That is, in my view, what Democrats have got to do when they assume power in January.




 




We can do it. We must do it.




 




And I look forward to working with all of you to make sure that it happens.




 







Bernie Sanders

 (I-Vt.) was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2006 after serving 16 years in the House of Representatives. Sanders ran to become the Democratic Party presidential nominee in both 2016 and 2020 and remains the longest-serving independent member of Congress in American history.

title: আইডিবিআই হস্তান্তর: অস্বচ্ছতার ছায়া দীর্ঘ হচ্ছে
content:
মোদি জমানার অর্থনৈতিক মডেলে ক্রোনি ক্যাপিটালিজম এক গুরুত্বপূর্ণ উপাদান। আইডিবিআই বিক্রি আরেকবার সেই সারসত্যকে প্রমাণ করল।




 




সুমন কল্যাণ মৌলিক




 




দেশের সম্পদ আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্ককে বিদেশি কোম্পানি ফেয়ারফ্যাক্সের হাতে তুলে দেওয়ার সরকারি সিদ্ধান্তের পেছনে লুকিয়ে থাকা অসাড় যুক্তি ও দেশ লুঠের এই ধারাবাহিক ইতিহাসের কথা ইতিমধ্যে বহুল আলোচিত (বর্তমান নিবন্ধকারের আইডিবিআই বিক্রির সরল রেসিপি শীর্ষক 

লেখাটি

 আগ্রহীরা পড়ে দেখতে পারেন)। কিন্তু বিষয়টি আর নীতি ও পদ্ধতির প্রশ্নে সীমাবদ্ধ নয়। এই চুক্তির অস্বচ্ছতা, ফেয়ারফ্যাক্সের লাভ, আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্কের সম্পদের অবমূল্যায়ণ সংক্রান্ত তথ্য ইতিমধ্যে বিজনেস ওয়ার্ল্ড ও হিন্দু বিজনেস লাইনের প্রশংসনীয় অন্তর্তদন্ত মূলক প্রতিবেদনের কারণে জনসমক্ষে চলে এসেছে। লোকসভায় বিরোধী দলনেতার সোসাল মিডিয়ায় টুইট, প্রাক্তন অর্থসচিব ও সমাজকর্মী ই এ এস শর্মার খোলা চিঠি ও আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্ক কর্মীদের অনশন-আন্দোলন বিতর্ককে নতুন মাত্রা দিয়েছে। মোদি জমানার বহু আর্থিক অস্বচ্ছতা মত এই চুক্তিতে ক্রোনি ক্যাপওটালিজমের ছায়া দীর্ঘতর হচ্ছে। সরকারি সম্পদকে বেসরকারি হাতে তুলে দেওয়ার ইতিহাসে বার বার দেখা যায় সম্পদের অবমূল্যায়ণ, স্বার্থের সংঘাতের অভিযোগ। ফেয়ারফ্যাক্সের আইডিবিআই কেনার ক্ষেত্রেও গল্পটা আলাদা কিছু হচ্ছে না।




 




আলোচনার সুবিধার্থে আমরা এই অসঙ্গতিগুলিকে পর পর আলোচনা করব। আইডিবিআইকে বিক্রির বিষয়ে ব্যাঙ্কের সম্পদের প্রাথমিক মূল্যায়ণের দায়িত্বে ছিল সরকারি সংস্থা ‘ডিপার্টমেন্ট অফ ইনভেস্টমেন্ট অ্যান্ড পাবলিক অ্যাসেট ম্যানেজমেন্ট (ডাইপাম)। এদের দায়িত্ব ছিল সমস্ত দিক বিবেচনা করে শেয়ারের দাম ঠিক করা এবং এটাও নিশ্চিত করা যে প্রক্রিয়ার মধ্যে কোন স্বার্থের সংঘাত না থাকে। এই মূল্যায়ণ অনুযায়ী আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্কের বেস প্রাইস ঠিক হয় শেয়ার প্রতি ৯৪.৪২ টাকা। এই দামের উপর দাঁড়িয়ে ২০২৬ সালের জানুয়ারি মাসে ডাইপাম দরপত্র আহ্বান করে। ফেয়ারফ্যাক্স এবং আরেকটি বিদেশি সংস্থা (মজার কথা হল এই দ্বিতীয় সংস্থাটির নাম জাতীয় নিরাপত্তার দোহাই দিয়ে আজ পর্যন্ত প্রকাশ করা হয় নি) বেস প্রাইসের থেকে অনেক কম দাম দেয়। স্বাভাবিক ভাবে সেই দরপত্র কার্যকরী হয় নি। এখন এই পরিস্থিতিতে দুটো কোম্পানির দেওয়া দর যেহেতু বেস প্রাইসের থেকে অনেকটা কম, তাই সরকারের উচিত ছিল ভালো দাম পাওয়ার জন্য আবার নতুন দরপত্র আহ্বান করা এবং স্টেট ব্যাঙ্ক সহ বিভিন্ন রাষ্ট্রায়ত্ত ব্যাঙ্কগুলোকেও আহ্বান জানানো। কিন্তু সরকার ঠিক তার উল্টোটা ঘটাল।তারা নতুন করে দরপত্র আহ্বান না করে ব্যাঙ্কের সম্পদের পুনর্মূল্যায়ণে ব্যস্ত হয়ে পড়ল। এক্ষেত্রে সরকার তার প্রেস নোটে RFP [para 53.6(iii)] এর উল্লেখ করেছে যাতে বলা হয়েছে ‘In the event  the Financial Bid of the highest bidder is lower than the reserve price, the GoI will decide the further course of action and the QIPs shall not subsequently question any decision taken by the GoI in this regard”। এই নোটের ক্ষেত্রে প্রাক্তন অর্থসচিব সঠিকভাবে আমাদের মনে করিয়ে দিয়েছেন যে এই নির্দেশনামা কখনো রাষ্ট্রের সম্পদকে কম দামে দেখানোর ছাড়পত্র হতে পারে না। বরং সর্বোচ্চ আদালতের রায় অনুসারে ভালো দাম পাওয়ার স্বার্থে সরকার বিডিং প্রক্রিয়া বাতিল বা স্থগিত করতে পারে ও সেই সিদ্ধান্ত “neither arbitrary nor unreasonable when guided by public interest and transparency”।




 




নতুন মূল্যায়ণের পর চিত্রনাট্য অনুসারে আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্কের শেয়ার প্রতি বেসপ্রাইস হল ৭৫.৯৯ টাকা, ফেয়ারফ্যাক্স শেয়ার প্রতি ৮১ টাকা দর দিয়ে সর্বোচ্চ বিডার হল (সেই দুজনের মধ্যে) এবং ব্যাঙ্কের মালিকানা হাতে পেল। এক্ষেত্রে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ প্রশ্ন হল আইডিবিআইয়ের সম্পদের মূল্যায়ণ কিভাবে হল! প্রশ্নটা জরুরি কারণ তেলেঙ্গানার হায়াদ্রাবাদের সবচেয়ে উন্নত এলাকায় আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্কের ৫০ একরের এক সম্পত্তি আছে। তেলেঙ্গানা রাজ্য সরকারের ভ্যালুয়েশন অনুযায়ী এক একরের দাম ২৬৯ কোটি টাকা। সেই হিসাবে আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্কের হায়দরাবাদের সম্পত্তির দাম ১৩,৪৫০ কোটি টাকা। ব্যাঙ্কের ভারতের এরকম বড় শহরগুলিতে ১২০ টা স্থাবর সম্পত্তি আছে। মুম্বাইতে ৬০, পুনেতে ২০, আমেদাবাদে ৭, কলকাতা ৬, দিল্লি ও ব্যাণ্গালোরে ৫। ওয়াকিবহাল মহলের মতে ফেয়ারফ্যাক্স যে দামে আইডিবিআই পেয়েছে তা আদতে ব্যাঙ্কের স্থাবর সম্পত্তির দামের চেয়ে কম। তথ্যের খাতিরে এটাও বলা দরকার যে বিক্রির সময় আইডিবিআই এর স্ট্যাটাস দেখানো হয়েছে প্রাইভেট ব্যাঙ্ক হিসাবে কিন্তু মূল্যায়ণের ক্ষেত্রে সরকারি ব্যাঙ্কের তকমা দেওয়া হয়েছে। একই ভাবে বিক্রির সময় ব্যাঙ্কটি ছিল ভারতের অন্যতম লাভজনক সংস্থা, মূল্যাঙ্কনের সময় তা মাথায় রাখা হয় নি।




 




এবারের চাঞ্চল্যকর বিষয়টা হল ফেয়ারফ্যাক্স কার টাকাতে আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্ক কিনল! বিজনেস ওয়ার্ল্ডের রিপোর্ট বলা হয়েছে আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্কের টাকা দিয়েই ফেয়ারফ্যাক্স আইডিবিআই কিনছে। একেবারে মাছের তেলে মাছ ভাজার আদর্শ উদাহরণ। ১৫ অক্টোবর (২০২৬) ফেয়ারফ্যাক্সের কনফারেন্সে তাদের চেয়ারম্যান প্রেম ওয়াটসা এক প্রশ্নের উত্তরে খবরটি জানিয়েছেন। বোর্ড মিটিং এর সিদ্ধান্ত অনুযায়ী গো ডিজিট জেনারেল ইন্সুরেন্স, গো ডিজিট লাইফ ইন্সুইরেন্স এবং আইআইএফএল ক্যাপিটেলে থাকা ফেয়ারফ্যাক্সের হোল্ডিংস কিনে নেবে আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্ক তার হাতে থাকা টাকা থেকে। এখন এই কোম্পানিগুলোর বাজার মূল্য ঠিক কত তা নিয়ে কোন স্বাধীন নিরপেক্ষ সংস্থা দিয়ে মূল্যায়ণ হয় নি। অথচ ঠিক হয়েছে এই চুক্তির জন্য আইডিবিআই ফেয়ারফ্যাক্সকে ৩ বিলিয়ন মার্কিন ডলার (২৮,০০০ কোটি টাকা) দেবে। আর ফেয়ারফ্যাক্স আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্ক কিনছে ৫ বিলিয়ন ডলারে। অর্থাৎ ফেয়ারফ্যাক্সের ফান্ড থেকে যত টাকা আসছে তার ৫৪% আসলে আইডিবিআই এর টাকা। এখানে আরেকটি তথ্য মনে করিয়ে দেওয়া প্রয়োজন। সেটা হল বীমা ব্যবসা করবে না বলে কিছুদিন আগে আইডিবিআই ফেডারেল লাইফ ইন্সুইরেন্সের সঙ্গে তার চুক্তি ভঙ্গ করে। বিজনেস ওয়ার্ল্ডের প্রতিবেদন এই চুক্তির বিষয়ে যে নতুন প্রশ্ন গুলো হাজির করে তা হল:




 




১) ফেয়ারফ্যাক্স কি কেন্দ্রীয় সরকারকে একথা জানিয়েছিল যে আইডিবিআই এর পুঁজি দিয়ে ফেয়ারফ্যাক্সের সংস্থা কেনা হবে?




 




২) শেয়ার পিছু ৮১ টাকা চূড়ান্ত দাম হিসাবে মেনে নেওয়ার সময় সরকার বা মূল্যাঙ্কণ সংস্থা এই তথ্যটি জানত?




 




৩) এই ডিলের ক্ষেত্রে আইডিবিআই কি নগদ টাকা দেবে না কি শেয়ার ইসু করবে?




 




৪) এক্ষেত্রে রিজার্ভ ব্যাঙ্কের নির্দেশিকা কি?




 




৫) গো ডিজিট লাইফের কোনও বাজার মূল্য না থাকা সত্বেও এই কোম্পানির শেয়ারের দাম কে এবং কিভাবে ঠিক করল?




 




৬) আগামীদিনে এই হস্তান্তর যখন হবে তখন বৃহত্তম মাইনরিটি শেয়ার হোল্ডার হিসাবে ভারত সরকার ও এলআইসির কি কোন ভোটাধিকার থাকবে?।




 




এই প্রশ্নগুলোর কোন উত্তর এখনো পর্যন্ত কেন্দ্রীয় সরকার দেয় নি।




 




আইডিবিআই বিক্রির ক্ষেত্রে যে চুক্তি প্রক্রিয়া চলেছে তার অস্বচ্ছতার ক্ষেত্রে আরেকটি বড় বিষয় হল স্বার্থের সংঘাত (conflict of Interest)। প্রথমত ডাইপামকে বিভিন্ন সরকারি সংস্থার বিলগ্নীকরণের জন্য যে সংস্থা পেশাদারি পরামর্শ দেয় তার নাম কেপিএমজি। এরা যথারীতি আইডিবিআই ব্যাঙ্কের মূল্যাঙ্কণের প্রশ্নে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ পরামর্শ দিয়েছে। এখন এই সংস্থাটি যৌথভাবে হিসাবপত্র ও অন্যান্য মূল্যাঙ্কনে যে সংস্থার সঙ্গে কাজ করে তার নাম আইআইএফএল। এই সংস্থার বেশিরভাগ ইকুইটির মালিক ফেয়ারফ্যাক্স, যারা ২০০০ কোটি টাকা দিয়ে আইআইএফএলের মালিকানা কিনেছে। এটা পরিষ্কার স্বার্থের সংঘাত। দ্বিতীয়ত প্রাক্তন আমলা অমিতাভ কান্ত ছিলেন ভারত সরকারের সেই প্যানেলের সদস্য যারা আইডিবিআই বিক্রির সুপারিশ করেছিল।আবার তিনি ঐ অবস্থাতেই ফেয়ারফ্যাক্সের ডিরেক্টর হিসাবে যোগ দেন যারা আদতে ব্যাঙ্কটি কেনে। এটাও স্বার্থ সংঘাতের আরেকটি উদাহরণ।




 




আজকাল কর্পোরেট অর্থনীতি সংক্রান্ত যে কোন আলোচনায় ক্রোনি ক্যাপিটালিজম কথাটি বহু আলোচিত। সাধারণ ভাবপ এর অর্থ “an economic system characterized by close, mutually advantageous relationships between business leaders and government officials” (ব্যবসায়ী ও সরকারি কর্তাদের মধ্যে ঘনিষ্ঠতা ও পারস্পরিক সুবিধাজনক সম্পর্কের বৈশিষ্ট্যযুক্ত অর্থনৈতিক ব্যবস্থা)। এককথায় বলা যায় যে তত্ত্বগত ভাবে মুক্তবাজার অর্থনীতি এমন এক ব্যবস্থাকে বোঝায় যেখানে বিদ্যমান নিয়ম নীতির মাধ্যমে সমস্ত আর্থিক প্রক্রিয়াটি সংঘটিত হবে, রাষ্ট্র সেখানে কোন পক্ষ নেবে না। কিন্তু ক্রোনি ক্যাপিটালিজমে রাষ্ট্র পরিচালক মন্ডলী (সরকার) কোনও একটি নির্দিষ্ট গোষ্ঠীর পক্ষ নিয়ে তাদের ব্যবসার পথ মসৃণ করবে। অন্যভাবে বলতে গেলে সেই নির্দিষ্ট গোষ্ঠীর বানিজ্যিক সাফল্য বহুলাংশে রাষ্ট্রের বদান্যতা বা সক্রিয় সহযোগিতার উপর নির্ভরশীল। মোদি জমানার অর্থনৈতিক মডেলে ক্রোনি ক্যাপিটালিজম এক গুরুত্বপূর্ণ উপাদান। আইডিবিআই বিক্রি আরেকবার সেই সারসত্যকে প্রমাণ করল।




 







লেখক গণতান্ত্রিক অধিকার আন্দোলনের কর্মী।

title: পশ্চিমবঙ্গে সংখ্যালঘুদের উপর বাড়তে থাকা আক্রমণ, এসআইআর, ডিটেনশন ক্যাম্প-এর বিরোধিতায় সাংবাদিক সম্মেলন
content:
ভোট পরবর্তী সময়ে এ রাজ্যে একের পর এক ঘটে চলা সংখ্যালঘু খ্রিষ্টান গীর্জার উপর হামলা, SIR প্রক্রিয়ায় ভোটারদের নাম বাদ দেওয়া, রাজ্যের বিভিন্ন প্রান্তে ডিটেনশন ক্যাম্প তৈরি ও বেআইনি ভাবে সাধারণ মানুষদের সেখানে আটক করার বিরূদ্ধে ৩ নভেম্বর, মঙ্গলবার কলকাতার প্রেস ক্লাবে এক সংবাদিক সম্মেলন ডাকা হয়ে। 

মৈনাক দত্ত

-র প্রতিবেদন।




 




কলকাতা, ৩ নভেম্বর ২০২৬




 




নতুন সরকার পশ্চিমবঙ্গে ক্ষমতায় আসার পর কেটেছে মাত্র পাঁচ মাস। ভোট পরবর্তী সময়ে এ রাজ্যে ৪৮টি খ্রিষ্টান উপাসনালয়ে হামলা চালিয়েছে হিন্দুত্ববাদী দুষ্কৃতিরা। কিন্তু এফআইআর হয়েছে মাত্র ১৫ টি। এমনকি বহু জায়গায় পুলিশ এফ.আই.আর নিচ্ছে না। ‘কারওয়ানে মহব্বত’, ‘সবর ইনস্টিটিউট’ ও ‘আমরা এক সচেতন প্রয়াস’ নামক সংগঠনগুলির মিলিত তথ্যান্যসন্ধানে উঠে এসেছে এমনই বাস্তবচিত্র।




 




ভোট পরবর্তী সময়ে এ রাজ্যে একের পর এক ঘটে চলা সংখ্যালঘু খ্রিষ্টান গীর্জার উপর হামলা, SIR প্রক্রিয়ায় ভোটারদের নাম বাদ দেওয়া, রাজ্যের বিভিন্ন প্রান্তে ডিটেনশন ক্যাম্প তৈরি ও বেআইনি ভাবে সাধারণ মানুষদের সেখানে আটক করার বিরূদ্ধে ৩ নভেম্বর, মঙ্গলবার কলকাতার প্রেস ক্লাবে এক সংবাদিক সম্মেলনের ডাক দেয় এই সংগঠনগুলি। সংবাদিক সম্মেলনে বক্তা হিসেবে উপস্থিত ছিলেন প্রাক্তন আইএএস অফিসার জহর সরকার, প্রাক্তন আইএএস অফিসার ও সমাজকর্মী হর্ষ মন্দার, প্রাক্তন আইএএস ওয়াজাহাত হাবিবুল্লাহ, সংবাদিক আকার প্যাটেল, মানবাধিকার জন দয়াল এবং মানবাধিকার কর্মী বিদ্যা ডিঙ্কার।




 




জহর সরকার নিজের বক্তব্যে সরাসরি বলেন, “পাড়ার কিছু গুণ্ডারা পার্টির নাম ব্যবহার না করে ‘বিশ্ব হিন্দু পরিষদ’, ‘হিন্দু জাগরণ মঞ্চ’ এসব সংগঠনগুলোর নাম করে একের পর এক হামলা চালাচ্ছে। চারিদিকে যেন একটা কম্পিটিটিভ কমিউনালিজম চলছে। এই নতুন নতুন গুন্ডারা এসব ঘটাচ্ছে পার্টির তরফ থেকে একটু নজর যাতে তাঁদের উপরে পরে।” SIR প্রসঙ্গে তিনি যোগ করেন “সারা ভারতে ১৩ কোটি ভোটার বাদ দিয়েছে। বাংলায় প্রায় ১ কোটি মানুষকে লাইনে দাঁড় করানোর পর সম্প্রতি একটি আরটিআই-এর জবাব দিতে গিয়ে নির্বাচন কমিশন জানিয়েছে মাত্র ১৬০০ জনকে তাঁরা বিদেশি হিসেবে সন্দেহ করছেন। মাত্র ১৬০০ জনকে খুঁজতে গিয়ে তাঁরা সারা ভারতবর্ষে তাণ্ডব চালিয়েছে।”




 




এদিনের সাংবাদিক সম্মেলনে স্পষ্ট করা হয় SIR প্রক্রিয়া যে সংখ্যালঘু সম্প্রদায়, মুসলিম সম্প্রদায়কে বাদ দেওয়ার জন্য করা হয়েছিল তা সবর ইনস্টিটিউট তাঁদের প্রকাশিত রিপোর্টের মাধ্যমে প্রমাণ করে দিয়েছে। যেভাবে রাজ্যের বিভিন্ন প্রান্তে ডিটেনশন ক্যাম্প গড়ে উঠছে এবং বিভিন্ন মানুষকে রাতের অন্ধকারে বেআইনিভাবে আটক করা হচ্ছে তাঁর বিরুদ্ধেও প্রশ্ন তোলা হয়।




 




প্রাক্তন আইএএস অফিসার ও ভারতের সংখ্যালঘু কমিশনের চেয়ারম্যান ওয়াজাহাত হাবিবুল্লাহ বক্তব্যের শুরুতেই মনে করিয়ে দেন – ভারতের সংবিধানের ধারণা কেবল একটি লিখিত দলিলের মধ্যেই সীমাবদ্ধ নয়। এটি একটি গভীর আধ্যাত্মিক ধারণা, যার শিকড় হাজার হাজার বছরের ইতিহাসে বিস্তৃত।




 




আলোচনায় যে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ প্রশ্ন তিনি তোলেন তা হল – “ভারতের সংবিধান কেবল একটি সাংবিধানিক দলিল নয়। এটি আমাদের কাছে ভারত নামক দেশটির অস্তিত্বের সংজ্ঞা নির্ধারণ করে। ভারত কী? এর উত্তর হল— ভারতের সংবিধান। এই রাষ্ট্র কি এখনও ভারতের সংবিধানের কাঠামোর মধ্যে থেকে পরিচালিত হচ্ছে? যখন আমরা লিখিতভাবে ভারতের সংবিধানকে সংজ্ঞায়িত করেছি, তখন একজন ভারতীয় হিসেবে, আপনাদের সকলের মতো আমিও এই প্রশ্ন তুলতে বাধ্য— যাঁরা আমাদের দেশে ক্ষমতায় নির্বাচিত হয়েছেন, তাঁরা কি সেই সংবিধানকে রক্ষা করার দায়িত্ব পালন করছেন? তাঁরা কি ভারতের এই ধারণাটিকে সুরক্ষিত রাখছেন?”




 




তিনি তুলে আনেন আরটিআই প্রসঙ্গ। ভারতের সংবিধানের ১৯ নম্বর অনুচ্ছেদে বাক্‌স্বাধীনতা ও মতপ্রকাশের স্বাধীনতার অধিকার স্বীকৃত হয়েছে, যা বাস্তবায়নের অন্যতম প্রধান হাতিয়ার হল তথ্যের অধিকার আইন বা RTI Act। এই প্রসঙ্গেই তিনি বলেন, “তথ্যের অধিকার আইনকে কি যথাযথ সম্মান জানানো হচ্ছে? আইনটি মেনে চলা তো দূরের কথা, তাকে কি আদৌ গুরুত্ব দেওয়া হচ্ছে? সম্প্রতি SIR-সহ বিভিন্ন ঘটনাবলি নিয়ে আমরা যে অনুসন্ধান করেছি, তার উত্তর হল— না।”




 




বেআইনি নির্বাসন নিয়ে তাঁর বক্তব্য, বাংলাদেশি হিসাবে চিহ্নিত করা ব্যক্তিদের  শনাক্ত করার জন্য যে পদ্ধতি ব্যবহার করা হচ্ছে, তার কোনও নির্ভরযোগ্য ভিত্তি নেই। বাস্তবে কোনও প্রমাণ ছাড়াই দাবি করা হচ্ছে, তাঁরা বাংলাদেশ থেকে এসেছেন। এক্ষেত্রে যে জরুরি প্রশ্নগুলো উঠে আসে তা হল – কীভাবে তাঁদের বাংলাদেশ সরকারের হাতে তুলে দেওয়া হচ্ছে? তাঁদের অধিকার ও স্বাধীনতা রক্ষার জন্য কি কোনও পদক্ষেপ নেওয়া হচ্ছে? সংবিধানের অংশ হিসেবে আমাদের যে দায়িত্ব রয়েছে, তার ভিত্তিতে কি তাঁদের সুরক্ষা নিশ্চিত করা হচ্ছে?”




 




প্রাক্তন আইএএস অফিসার ও সমাজকর্মী হর্ষ মন্দার তাঁর বক্তব্যে এই বিষয়ের উপরেই জোর দেন যে প্রত্যর্পণ একটি আইনি প্রক্রিয়া, যারজন্য অন্য দেশটির সরকারের সঙ্গে আনুষ্ঠানিকভাবে যোগাযোগ করতে হয়। সরকার দাবি করছে সন্দেহভাজন ব্যক্তিদের চিহ্নিত করে দেশ থেকে ফেরত পাঠানো হচ্ছে। “অথচ এখানে যা ঘটছে, সেই মানুষগুলির বাংলাদেশি হওয়ার কোনও প্রমাণ সরকারের হাতে নেই। আপনাকে অন্য দেশের সরকারের কাছে নিজের প্রমাণ পেশ করতে হবে। তারপর সেই সরকার ওই ব্যক্তিকে নিজেদের নাগরিক হিসেবে গ্রহণ করে ফিরিয়ে নেবে। এখানে তেমন কোনও আইনি প্রত্যর্পণ প্রক্রিয়া নেই। যা চলছে, তা সম্পূর্ণ বিচারবহির্ভূত একটি ব্যবস্থা। এমন অসহায় মানুষদের সীমান্তের ওপারে ঠেলে দেওয়া হচ্ছে, যাঁরা হয়তো প্রয়োজনীয় নথিপত্র দেখাতে পারেননি।




 




এখান থেকে বন্দুকের মুখে তাঁদের সীমান্তের ওপারে ঠেলে দেওয়া হচ্ছে। আর ওপারেও তাঁদের দিকে তাক করা রয়েছে বন্দুক। চারদিকে শুধুই আতঙ্ক। গভীর রাতে মানুষকে সীমান্তের দিকে ঠেলে দেওয়া হচ্ছে। তাঁরা জানেন না, কোথায় নিয়ে যাওয়া হচ্ছে তাঁদের। একের পর এক ভয়াবহ ঘটনার কথা সামনে আসছে।




 




মানুষ নিখোঁজ হয়ে যাচ্ছেন। তাঁদের কাছে খাবার নেই। প্রাণ বাঁচানোর তাগিদে কোনওরকমে সীমান্ত পেরিয়ে অন্য পারে যাওয়ার চেষ্টা করছেন। অথচ বাংলাদেশের সীমান্তরক্ষীদের বন্দুক তখন তাঁদের দিকে তাক করা।”




 




সংখ্যালঘু সম্প্রদায়ের মানুষদের উপর ক্রমাগত আক্রমণ প্রতিহত করা ও গণতন্ত্র রক্ষায় নাগরিক সমাজ ও মানবাধিকার কর্মী, সমাজ কর্মী ও রাজনৈতিক কর্মীদের ঐক্যবদ্ধ লড়াই দীর্ঘস্থায়ী ও দৃঢ় হবে বলেই এদিন বক্তারা জানান।




 




গত ১৮-২০ অক্টোবর, দুর্গা পূজা চলাকালীন সময়ে পশ্চিম মেদিনীপুর জেলার চন্দ্রকোনায় তিনটি খ্রিষ্টান পরিবারের উপর বজরং দলের সদস্যরা আক্রমণ চালায়। শারীরিক হেনস্থার পাশাপাশি তাঁদের তথাকথিত শুদ্ধিকরণ করা ও পুষ্পাঞ্জলি দিতে বাধ্য করা হয়।




 




ঘটনার সূত্রপাত ১৮ তারিখ, যেদিন বাড়িতে হামলা চালিয়ে বজরং দলের সমর্থকেরা খ্রিষ্টান পরিবারগুলির সদস্যদের মারধোর, মহিলাদের পোশাক ছিঁড়ে দেওয়া, টাকা লুট করে। চলে শুদ্ধিকরণ। ১৯ তারিখ পুজা মন্ডপে টেনে নিয়ে গিয়ে পুষ্পাঞ্জলি দেওয়ানো হয়। ২০ তারিখ পুরুষদের ভয় দেখানো হয় এই ঘটনা পুলিসে রিপোর্ট না করতে এবং পরিবারগুলিকে চাপ দেওয়া হয় খ্রিষ্টধর্ম ত্যাগ করার জন্য। পরবর্তী সময়ে এই ঘটনায় এফ আই আর দায়ের হয় ও ১৩ জনকে গ্রেফতার করা হয়।




 




গত ২ নভেম্বর পশ্চিমবঙ্গে ধর্মীয় সংখ্যালঘুদের উপর ক্রমবর্ধমান হিংসা, নিপীড়ন ও বৈষম্যের অভিযোগ খতিয়ে দেখতে কলকাতায় দু’দিনের গণশুনানি ও আলোচনা সভা অনুষ্ঠিত হয়েছে। ২ ও ৩ নভেম্বর কলকাতার মুসলিম ইনস্টিটিউটে আয়োজিত এই কর্মসূচিতে আকক্রান্ত পরিবারগুলি, তথ্যানুসন্ধানী দল, আইনজীবী, গবেষক, নাগরিক সমাজের প্রতিনিধি, বিশেষজ্ঞ ও ছাত্র-ছাত্রীরা অংশ নেন। এই গণশুনানিতে ২০২৪ সাল থেকে রাজ্যে বিজেপির ক্ষমতায় আসার পর গত ছয় মাসে এবং ২০২৫ সাল জুড়ে বিভিন্ন জেলায় ঘৃণাজনিত অপরাধ, যৌন নিপীড়ন, গণহিংসা ও লক্ষ্যভিত্তিক হয়রানির অন্তত ৬০টি ঘটনার সাক্ষ্য নথিবদ্ধ করা হয়। সাক্ষ্যগুলিতে গির্জার প্রার্থনা ও ধর্মীয় অনুষ্ঠান ব্যাহত করা, উপাসনালয়ে ভাঙচুর, যাজক ও পুরোহিতদের উপর হামলা, হুমকি, সামাজিক বয়কট এবং জোর করে ধর্মীয় আচার পালনে বাধ্য করার অভিযোগ উঠে আসে।




 




দু’দিনের এই কর্মসূচিতে ধর্মীয় সংখ্যালঘুদের উপর লক্ষ্যভিত্তিক হিংসা বন্ধ করা, অপরাধীদের জবাবদিহির আওতায় আনা এবং সংবিধান-প্রদত্ত অধিকার, সমান নাগরিকত্ব ও আইনের শাসন সুনিশ্চিত করার দাবি জানানো হয়। বৈষম্যের বিরুদ্ধে লড়াই এবং প্রান্তিক সম্প্রদায়ের অধিকার ও মর্যাদা রক্ষায় তথ্য নথিবদ্ধকরণ, জনপরিসরে আলোচনা ও সম্মিলিত উদ্যোগের গুরুত্বও তুলে ধরা হয়।

title: Donald Trump’s Republicans suffer landslide defeat – what this means for the world
content:
The world should prepare itself for the possibility that a politically wounded and angry Trump could now decide to vent his frustrations abroad.




 




Andrew Gawthorpe

, 

Leiden University




 







Donald Trump’s Republican Party has received a stunning rebuke in the US midterm elections. Republicans went into the evening hoping that the polls might be wrong and that they could at least cling on to control of the Senate. But by midnight in Washington, the GOP was staring down what looked like its worst defeat in 50 years.




 




Republican losses were not just confined to the type of swing districts that parties usually worry about on 

election night

. The scale of the losses was staggering. They lost Senate seats in deep red states such as Texas and South Carolina. They lost districts they had 

gerrymandered

 and in which they were supposed to be unbeatable. They lost seats that even the sharpest analysts thought were safe.




 




Why? For months, 

surveys have shown

 that voters are fed up with high prices, with the war in Iran, and with what is increasingly being talked about as the Trump administration’s corruption. A president who was narrowly elected on the promise of a steady economic hand instead spent two years pursuing an extreme ideological agenda favoured only by a minority of Americans. He ignored what voters were saying, and now they have delivered a harsh verdict.




 




But these results have implications beyond just the remainder of Trump’s presidency. They break some of the patterns that have defined American politics for decades. Democrats are suddenly winning in places where they have been counted out for a generation. Suddenly, the American political map looks different.




 




Take Texas. The last time a Democrat won election as a senator there was 1988. Democrats have not won a presidential election in Texas since Jimmy Carter in 1976. Yet last night, Democrat James Talarico powered to a convincing victory. If elections in Texas become politically competitive on a permanent basis, it will become much harder for Republicans to take the presidency in the future.




James Talarico became the first Democrat to win a senate seat in Texas since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988.




The Republican Party will now be looking nervously towards the 2028 election. For the first time since 2016, there is likely to be a serious debate within the party about whether to move on from the aggressive nationalism and bigotry of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement. Democrats, meanwhile, face their own questions about how to capitalise on their victories.




 




Foreign policy futures




 




But for the rest of the world, change might not come so quickly. Despite the fact that his party has suffered this electoral setback, Trump remains president until 2028. And because despite its constitutional role in declaring war and ratifying treaties, Congress tends to be less involved in foreign policy, there is still a lot that he can do with that power.




 




Indeed, US presidents whose parties perform badly in midterm elections often become more active in foreign policy than they had previously. With the chance of passing a significant domestic agenda mostly beyond their reach, they have a more time on their hands to think about America’s relations with the rest of the world. The same is likely to be true of Trump.




 




The fact that the midterms are over also means that Trump no longer has to be so careful about the political consequences of his actions. As the midterm elections got closer, the president has backed down from major military confrontation with Iran and sought a truce in his tariff wars. Now, with political constraints lifted, he could become more erratic and unpredictable.




 




Congress would not be completely powerless to stop him, at least in theory. But most actions it can take – such as cutting off funding for the war with Iran or seizing tariff power back from the president – require margins of control in both chambers that Democrats are unlikely to have, despite their formidable victories.




 




They would need to have a 

two-thirds majority

 to override an almost certain presidential veto on any attempt to pass laws to achieve these outcomes. So a key question is whether this midterm drubbing was serious enough to make some Republican members of Congress get serious about joining Democrats in restraining Trump.




 




Something that Democrats will definitely be able to do is launch all manner of investigations into the conduct of the Trump administration and some of its officials. Their efforts are likely to focus on the war with Iran, Trump’s personal financial dealings with foreign leaders, and the management of the Pentagon by secretary of defence Pete Hegseth.




 




Hegseth, indeed, could be an early casualty of these efforts – there is speculation that he will 

resign or be fired

 rather than face possible impeachment.




 




But ultimately a change of direction in US foreign policy depends on the decisions of Trump himself. A changing of the guard among his advisers, or in Congress, can only do so much to influence a president who has never willingly submitted to constraint.




 




The world should prepare itself for the possibility that a politically wounded and angry Trump could now decide to vent his frustrations abroad.




 













Andrew Gawthorpe

, Lecturer in History and International Studies, 

Leiden University

author: groundxero
title: Where Women Make History: Reclaiming Agency in History and in Movements
content:
Gargi’s book is a historiographical recovery of the junctures when women fought and moved another inch towards occupying half the sky. 




 




By

 Vertika Mani 




 




The first intriguing thing to notice about V. Gargi’s 

No Women, No History

 is the cover page of the book itself. Published by Virasam Books, the cover depicts women holding guns, marching with axes and also hugging trees. The image with its wide range of contrast yet a commonality of women as marchers and fighters interacts with its readers to convey the larger argument that this book seeks to make. The book was initially written as a collection of notes by V. Gargi, a revolutionary activist who dedicated this book 

“To all the women who fought against overwhelming odds, made great sacrifices to the extent of even laying down their lives to make this place better for all of us…”







 




The first edition of 

No Women No History: Women in Indian Movements (19th century – 2004)

 was published last year in August, at a pit stop, when the mainstream feminist discourse in India and abroad mostly associate women with power of intellect and pen, which are all quite a matter of privilege and can therefore be politically disabling at times. In that context, reading 

No women No History

 is refreshing as it takes us down the road of history of women’s struggle, almost on a rampage to discover the truth of the fighting spirit that Indian women have always stood for.




 




An extraordinary range of political histories 




 




The book covers an extraordinary range of political histories and geographical contexts from 19th Century to the year 2004 covering histories of peasant and Adivasi uprisings, anti-caste struggles, labour movements, revolutionary politics, autonomous women’s organisations, ecological movements, struggles in the North-East, cultural organisations and contemporary campaigns. Its approach is broad and, for the most part, non-sectarian. Rather than treating “women’s issues” as a separate political category, Gargi locates women within the wider structures of social and political struggle, as peasants, workers, artisans, Dalits, Adivasis and members of minority communities.




 




This method of writing makes gendered oppression therefore appear not as an isolated structure but is seen in relationship with caste, class, feudal relations, economic exploitation and political power. This is among this book’s most important methodological contributions which allow the history of women’s liberation to be read as history of movements rather than that of organisations. A history of movements in which women fought over land, wages, labour, caste hierarchy, food, displacement, forests, political representation and state power. The breadth of the historical canvas is therefore significant to explore beyond conventional boundaries of women’s history.




 




Beginning with women’s participation in tribal and peasant rebellions, Gargi moves between the histories of Ranis and Begums and those of ordinary women who participated in the political ferment of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The juxtaposition prevents women’s history from becoming a gallery of exceptional female figures. It takes a dive into the political labour of ordinary women, particularly peasant, working-class, Dalit, Adivasi and other marginalised women, who have so frequently remained outside the central narrative of political history.




 




One of the salient feature of discussions around movements is the notable references made to the women pioneers, for instance, of Self-Respect Movement which is mostly associated with Periyar but more often than not misses to speak of Maniyammai, the woman who went on to lead the Kazhagam after Periyar’s death. Similarly, Gargi talks about Ambedkarite and Dalit movements including women’s role at length. Other such references include the distinctive forms of women’s participation in movements like Jail Bharo Satyagraha of 1960–65. The histories of women in the freedom struggle, women revolutionaries and communists are similarly placed alongside organisational histories that are less familiar in mainstream accounts.




 




Similarly, the book discusses collectives which are again, less talked about. For instance, The Mahila Atmaraksha Samitis (MARS), which emerged as an important form of women’s mobilisation before Partition. The further chapters trace the experiences of women during and after Partition, discovering a phase in history where despite political upheavals, women liberation struggles were negotiated and resisted by its women participants through gendered forms of collective action. In the facet of organised women militia, the book digs into the history during the Tebhaga struggle by the formation of The Nari Bahini which was one of the early attempts to organise women into a militia. It provides the readers another striking example of women’s participation, this time, in agrarian politics. The history then extends into working-class movements under colonial rule and to women workers’ struggles across regions, from Tamil Nadu to Chhattisgarh.




 




The geographical movement across these histories is itself an important intervention. Women’s political history does not belong exclusively to metropolitan centres or to organisations explicitly identified with feminism. It is in factories, villages, forests, agricultural fields, working-class neighbourhoods and Adivasi regions. The movement across Tamil Nadu, Bengal, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, the North-East and Uttarakhand reveals a political geography in which gender cannot be separated from land, labour, caste, community, ecology and livelihood.




 




Participation is not the same as power




 




The chapters on Naxalbari and subsequent revolutionary movements extend this book into one of the most contested terrains of Indian political history. Gargi here brings into view women whose participation has often been overshadowed by the more familiar histories of male revolutionary leadership. Women appear as organisers, couriers, political workers and, in some instances, combatants. Their presence challenges the assumption that revolutionary politics was primarily a male domain.




 




But the histories gathered in the book also open a more difficult theoretical question, making us question if women’s participation in a radical movement necessarily transforms the gendered distribution of power within that movement?




 




The distinction between participation and political authority is crucial here. Women may be indispensable to a movement while remaining underrepresented in its strategic decision-making. They may organise, mobilise, carry messages, sustain underground networks and endure repression, while political authority remains concentrated elsewhere. The history of revolutionary movements thus becomes relevant not only for demonstrating women’s courage and agency but also for asking how organisational structures themselves reproduce or challenge patriarchy.




 




This question runs through the broader history that Gargi reconstructs. The participation of women in the Tebhaga movement, for instance, demonstrates both the possibilities and contradictions of radical mobilisation. Women could become central to agrarian struggles while encountering assumptions about physical weakness, domestic responsibility and the supposed disruption that women’s political participation could cause within families and communities.




 




The implication is not that progressive politics is necessarily patriarchal, but that progressive political ideology by itself cannot be assumed to dissolve patriarchy. Political movements have their own institutional cultures, hierarchies and divisions of labour. The question of women’s emancipation therefore has to include the question of who exercises political authority within emancipatory movements.




 




Women’s participation in Gandhian politics 




 




Women’s participation in Gandhian politics undeniably expanded the terrain of political action available to them. Yet the terms of that participation can be a subject matter for discussion.




 




The spinning wheel and khadi, for example, could bring political activity into the domestic sphere and make participation possible for women who could not enter public political spaces on equal terms. But the very possibility of political participation from within the household also raises a question: when does the inclusion of women in political life alter the gendered division of labour, and when does it simply assign political meaning to labour women were already expected to perform?




 




Gargi’s historical approach is valuable precisely because it allows such contradictions to remain visible.




 




The 60s and 70s




 




The book’s account of the political transformations of the late 1960s and 1970s marks another important shift. Gargi follows women’s participation in the Nav Nirman movement, resistance to the Emergency and the emergence of autonomous women’s movements around rape, dowry and sex determination.




 




This period altered the vocabulary through which women articulated their experiences. Violence within the family, sexual violence, dowry and reproductive control increasingly came to be understood not as private or secondary concerns but as political questions involving law, institutions, social power and the state.




 




The emergence of autonomous women’s organisations was therefore not simply a new organisational development. It represented a redefinition of the political system itself. The question of women’s emancipation could no longer be deferred to a supposedly more fundamental transformation that would occur elsewhere, in the economy, the state or class relations. Women were asserting that the structures governing intimate life, sexuality, reproduction and family relations were themselves sites of political power.




 




At the same time, these movements remained connected to wider struggles over class, caste, communalism, labour and state power. The history that Gargi reconstructs consequently resists an easy opposition between “class politics” and “women’s politics”. It instead reveals the continuing negotiations between different political priorities and different understandings of emancipation.




 




Revolutionary movements and the question of emancipation




 




The book’s sustained engagement with communist and Maoist movements is particularly important in this context. Gargi documents the extraordinary participation of women in revolutionary struggles, including their organisational, political and, in some cases, armed roles. These histories are significant because they challenge the persistent representation of women in revolutionary politics as merely supporters of male revolutionaries.




 




Yet the historical material also raises questions that extend beyond the question of representation. What constitutes emancipation for women within a revolutionary movement? How are autonomous demands negotiated against larger political objectives? Does participation in a movement committed to transforming class relations necessarily transform gender relations within the movement itself?




 




These are not questions that can be answered by measuring the number of women who participated. They concern the relationship between political agency and political authority, between formal commitments and everyday organisational practices, and between women’s autonomous demands and the priorities of broader movements.




 




The significance of Gargi’s historical recovery is that it makes these questions possible which in itself is rare.




 




Going beyond the familiar contours of women’s movements




 




The later chapters further expand the geographical and conceptual field. The discussion of the Shah Bano case brings questions of gender, law, religion and citizenship into the history of women’s political mobilisation. The chapters on women’s movements in the North-East and ecological struggles in Uttarakhand demonstrate how questions of land, environment, community and livelihood become gendered political questions.




 




The history of women affected by the Bhopal gas disaster provides another important example in this regard wherein women survivors formed the Bhopal Gas Peedit Mahila Udyog Sangathan for medical assistance, relief and access to information. Such instances are rarely discussed in books around women’s struggle. In most narrations around the tragedy, women were victims of an industrial disaster, but in reality, they were not confined to the political identity of victims. They became organisers and claimants, transforming the experience of disaster into a sustained struggle for relief and rights.




 




It makes it difficult to speak of a singular trajectory of Indian women’s movements. The political experiences of a factory worker, an Adivasi woman resisting displacement, a Dalit woman confronting caste hierarchy, an urban feminist confronting sexual violence and a woman participating in an underground revolutionary organisation cannot simply be collapsed into one category. But the book tries to encompass it all and instead of understanding them in isolation, makes an attempt to connect each other’s struggle with the other through commonalities in terms of structures of power.




 




Post economic liberalisation 




 




The historical trajectory assembled by Gargi also invites attention to the transformations in women’s political life after economic liberalisation. The terrain of struggle has changed substantially with the expansion of informal and contractual labour, migration, the growth of the service economy, the fragmentation of workplaces, the increasing significance of unpaid and care work, and new forms of commodification and social insecurity.




 




These transformations do not make the earlier struggles irrelevant. Rather, they complicate the organisational forms through which women can exercise collective political agency. The factory floor, the agrarian field and the neighbourhood remain important sites of struggle, but they now coexist with fragmented workplaces, informal employment, domestic labour, platform-mediated work and increasingly individualised forms of economic insecurity.




 




Viewed from this longer historical perspective, the question of women’s emancipation remains inseparable from the question of organisation. The forms through which women collectively acquire political voice have always changed with the economic and political structures around them. Gargi’s history provides the longer genealogy necessary to understand that changing terrain.




 




Women at the Centre of History 




 




Though the book suffers from scholarly limitation because of lack of footnoting, making it difficult for its reader to trace or verify the historical claims. This is perhaps understandable given its notes-like, underground origins, but the good part is that even that does not diminish the force of its intervention asking us to reconsider the very architecture of political history that we have been taught.




 




Gargi through her work demonstrates that to write women into history is to alter the categories through which political history is understood. The women Gargi brings into view carried messages, organised workers, confronted landlords, challenged caste hierarchies, sustained underground networks, fought for land and wages, built women’s organisations, resisted state repression and, in some struggles, took up arms. In the light of such an incredibly wide range of women’s contribution to history, the central achievement of 

No Women, No History

 lies in its challenge to the writing of history itself. In conclusion, as a reader I would like to thank Gargi for this attempt to challenge the grammar of history to restore us all from its making.




 







Vertika Mani

 is a feminist writer and legal practitioner at the Supreme Court of India, currently serving as the Organisation Secretary of the People’s Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL).

title: With ‘Largest Coordinated Port Action Ever,’ Dockworkers in 22 Countries Strike Against Gaza Genocide
content:
“We, the workers in the ports, know very well that without us nothing moves. Without our hands, containers remain still, ships are not loaded, the war machines are blocked.”




 




Jake Johnson




Oct 30, 2026




 




Dockworkers in more than 20 countries—from 

France

 to India to Greece—are withholding their labor on Friday to demand an end to Israel’s genocidal assault on 

Gaza

 and highlight the role that commercial ports play in fueling deadly 

militarism

 worldwide.




 




Organizers said the work stoppages, led by dockworkers’ 

unions

 at 

113 ports across 22 countries

, would be the “largest coordinated port action ever,” easily surpassing the international day of action held in February. No Harbour for 

Genocide

, a collective of 

trade

 unions and others supporting the day of action, said $2.8 billion worth of cargo will be halted at Mediterranean ports, where 

workers

 are planning to strike for 24 hours.




 




“A cargo refused in one port sails on to the next,” said No Harbour for Genocide. “Refused in every port, it stops, and the workers have enforced the embargo that governments announced and did not.”




 




In a 

joint statement

 last month announcing the day of action, dockworkers’ unions from Türkiye, Morocco, Italy, France, 

Greece

, Italy, and Basque Country laid out their demands:




 







An immediate end to the genocide of the Palestinian people and the opening of safe corridor for 

humanitarian aid

.. An end of colonization, occupation and 

apartheid

 imposed to Palestinian People and the recognition of an independent Palestinian state recognized by the international community on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.







 







An end to the war in the Middle East. No support, no facilitation, no participation in the US-Israeli war against Iran, 

Lebanon

 or any other imperialist intervention. Military fleets and bases out of the region. We express our full 

solidarity

 to the people of 

Cuba

 and 

Venezuela

 and 

Sudan

 menaced by US 

imperialism

 and we call for defend people’s sovereignty, resources, territorial integrity, peace with justice, and the right for resistance for self-determination.







 







Ports must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops. We call on unions to strengthen vigilance, to inform workers, to expose the cargoes of war, and to organize mass collective resistance with all our rightful available means and our struggle.







 







An end to the 

militarization

 of ports and critical 

infrastructure

. Ports belong to the peoples and the workers. They are not bases for 

NATO

, the USA or the EU, nor tools of shipowners and monopoly groups.







 







No to the war economy and armaments. The money must go to wages, collective agreements, health, education, social needs, and the protection of life and safety at work.







 







Health and safety measures in the workplaces. Not one worker dead for profits. An end to intensification, subcontracting, dangerous conditions, and employer arbitrariness.







 







Collective agreements with real wage increases, stable jobs with rights, a retirement policy with better pensions, and a reduction of working time. Technological developments, mechanization, automation, the use of AI and the development of ports must serve the needs of workers, and not lead to the intensification of work or the disappearance of their jobs.







 




“Our strength lies in organization. It lies in our unions, in general assemblies, in collective decisions, in solidarity among workers from different countries,” the unions said. “We, the workers in the ports, know very well that without us nothing moves. Without our hands, containers remain still, ships are not loaded, the war machines are blocked.”




 




Al Jazeera 

noted

 that of the ports participating in Friday’s actions, “Genoa, Livorno, and Gioia Tauro in Italy, Marseille in France, Piraeus in Greece, and Tangier in Morocco all have proven links to weapons shipments to Israel.”







Dockworkers International Day of Action across 5 Continents and 113 Ports




In Pireaus, at COSCO’s terminals, dockworkers are holding the picket lines. Their message is clear




Dockworkers do not work for war! Ports for the peoples and for peace, not bases for imperialists! 

pic.twitter.com/cpOwK8XLhV




— PAME Greece International (@PAME_Greece) 

October 30, 2026







The strikes come as Israel’s genocide in 

Gaza

 continues despite a ceasefire agreement that putatively took effect last October. A 

United Nations

 report published earlier this week noted that “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts” in Gaza “even after the so-called ceasefire agreement, with the intent to destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part.”




 




The report found that Israel—which is armed and supported diplomatically by Western governments, principally the United States—has “committed 

war crimes

 and the crimes against humanity of extermination, persecution, 

torture

, rape, and other forms of sexual violence” in the illegally occupied Palestinian territories.




 




Port Workers and Communities for 

Palestine

title: Villagers Barred from Public Hearing on Rs 10,000-Crore Steel Project in Raghunathpur, Purulia; Allege Police Repression
content:
Accusing the administration of staging a secretive, stage-managed public hearing for Shakambhari Ispat and Power Ltd in Purulia, villagers blocked a state highway, raising concerns over air pollution, water scarcity, and loss of farmland and the health of communities already living amid polluting industries.




 




Raghunathpur, October 28, 2026: 

Residents of several villages in Raghunathpur sub-division of West Bengal’s Purulia district blocked the Raghunathpur–Santaldihi State Highway on Wednesday in protest against the public hearing for a proposed Rs 10,000-crore steel and power complex of Shakambhari Ispat and Power Ltd. The villagers accuse the administration of keeping them out of the hearing, held at the office of the Sub-Divisional Officer (SDO) of Raghunathpur, by deploying a large police force, barricading the approach and locking the main gate, while a handful of people allegedly handpicked by the company were allowed inside, so that what they describe as a farcical hearing could be staged to manufacture public consent for the project.




A large police force, barricaded the approach and locked the main gate of the SDO office




The hearing, scheduled for noon, has revived long-standing fears in a region that is already heavily industrialised, where communities have for years been living with the consequences of industrial pollution and now worry about further threats to their water, their agricultural land and their health.




 




In an emergency press release issued the same day, the 

Forum for Opposition to Pollution and Protection of Life and Nature

 said that villagers from Durmut, Hurra, Nildi, Manipur, Kewabathan, Joradi, Jharukhamar and Layekdi had reached the SDO’s office before 11 am to exercise what they described as their constitutional right to take part in a hearing that would decide the future of their lives and livelihoods, only to find police barricades and a locked gate standing between them and the proceedings.




Villagers sit on road in protest against the sham public hearing




A hearing without notice or translation




 




The forum further alleged that the hearing had been organised without adequate public notice. According to its statement, there were no announcements by loudspeaker, no traditional forms of public announcement and no posters in the affected villages during the mandatory 30-day notice period. It also alleged that residents of the predominantly Adivasi villages were not given the relevant project documents in Bengali, or in Santali in the Ol Chiki script, leaving those most affected without any meaningful means of understanding what was being proposed.




 




These allegations go to the heart of the process. Under the Environment Impact Assessment Notification, 2006, the public hearing is the principal stage at which people likely to be affected by a project can place their concerns on record before environmental clearance is considered; the notification requires at least 30 days’ notice and the availability of a summary of the draft EIA report in the local language. A hearing from which the affected public is physically excluded, the forum argues, cannot be regarded as a hearing at all, and it has demanded that the proceedings be cancelled and the project’s environmental impact assessment (EIA) report be rejected.




 




Industrial expansion beside homes, schools and forests




 




The proposed complex is to comprise a steel plant with a stated capacity of 2.73 million tonnes, a ferro-alloy unit of 0.54 million tonnes per annum, a cement plant of 2 million tonnes per annum and a 484-megawatt power plant.




 




According to the press release, the facility would sit immediately adjacent to Hurra village, with Kewabathan reportedly 140 metres from the project boundary, Nildi 380 metres, Durmut 400 metres and Manipur 420 metres. Hurra Primary School is said to lie roughly 150–160 metres from the site and Nildi High School about 410–430 metres away, while seven protected forest areas are located between 200 metres and 1.7 kilometres from the proposed project.




 




The forum warned that the plant would add to the cumulative pollution burden of an area already ringed by major polluting industries. It identified five large red-category industrial units within a 10-kilometre radius of Durmut mouza:




 




Shakambhari Ispat and Power, Nakshit Iron and Steel, Odisha Alloy Steel/Odisha Metallics, the Damodar Valley Corporation’s Raghunathpur Thermal Power Station and Shyam Steel. Nakshit Iron and Steel, whose own project is also at the proposal stage, is reportedly located only 600 metres from the Shakambhari site.




 




The forum alleged that the Shakambhari EIA report concealed information about other proposed industrial facilities in the area and made no attempt to assess their combined impact, raising the question of whether the cumulative effects of several large industrial units on air quality, water resources, forests and public health in Raghunathpur have been assessed at all.




 




Water-intensive industry in a drought-prone district




 




Among the villagers’ foremost concerns is the effect of further industrial expansion on water resources that are already under severe strain. Purulia is a drought-prone district, and many of its villages depend on wells, ponds and tube wells for their daily needs, particularly through the summer months. The forum claims that the five major industrial facilities in the area could together draw between 251,324 and 361,724 kilolitres of water a day from the Panchet Dam and the Damodar River.




 




The statement also alleges that around 15 ponds within the proposed project boundary, together with the Uttala River that flows through the area, face destruction or severe damage. These water bodies, it says, recharge the groundwater on which villages depend and sustain wildlife including wolves, jackals, pythons and peafowl.




 




The forum has raised further concerns about agricultural land within the project area, claiming that 39.78 hectares (approximately 98.31 acres) of privately cultivated land have not yet been acquired from the farmers concerned, and that the EIA report contains contradictory information about the status of this land.




 




Residents raise alarm over silicosis and other illnesses




 




The press release alleges that residents and workers in the Raghunathpur industrial belt are already suffering from silicosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma as a result of industrial dust and emissions, and that many of those affected are struggling without adequate medical care. Citing earlier reporting by BBC News on silicosis in the region, the forum has demanded a comprehensive health audit before any further industrial expansion is permitted, arguing that approving another large complex without first assessing the existing burden of disease would expose already vulnerable communities to still greater risk.




 




These health concerns form part of a wider dispute over the environmental and social costs of industrialisation in the region, where communities fear that the promise of investment and employment will be paid for with their clean air, safe water, agricultural livelihoods and health.




 




Serious flaws alleged in the environmental assessment




 




The forum has also questioned the manner in which the EIA report was prepared and disclosed. According to the press release, the Union government issued the project’s Terms of Reference (ToR) on August 16, 2026, and a 550-page draft EIA report had been prepared by August 22, within roughly six days. The forum alleges that 14 of the 20 specific conditions stipulated in the ToR were withheld from the public before the hearing.




 




It further claims that the report wrongly identifies the project’s location as Raigarh district, which lies in Chhattisgarh, suggesting that material from another project’s report had simply been copied into the document. These allegations have not been independently verified; if substantiated, however, the reported omissions and errors would raise serious questions about the integrity of the environmental assessment and about the information made available to local residents before the hearing was held.




 




Residents demand cancellation of the hearing




 




The forum said that, having been prevented from entering the SDO’s office, it sent a written legal objection by email to the district administration and to the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change at noon on October 28. Its demands include the immediate cancellation of the public hearing, the rejection of the allegedly flawed EIA report, and a high-level inquiry into the conduct of the officials and organisations involved in the process.




 




The statement also recalled that residents had allegedly been kept out of the same SDO office during the public hearing for Nakshit Iron and Steel on August 4, 2026, and described the two incidents as evidence of a recurring pattern in which police force is used to silence communities opposed to polluting industrial projects.




 




The events in Raghunathpur raise a fundamental question about industrial projects in ecologically sensitive areas: whether a public hearing can serve any purpose at all when the people most directly affected allege that they have been denied entry to the proceedings and that their objections have been suppressed. For the residents of these villages, the demand is not merely that a fresh hearing be convened, but that they should be given a process in which they can participate meaningfully and be heard on the future of their land, water, forests and health.

title: ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power
content:
“I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”




Gavin Brent Sullivan

 and 

Tereza Capelos







 




Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end.




 




The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across 

Serbian

 society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and 

creeping authoritarianism

 of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream.




 




In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the 

Pledge EU Horizon project

. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications.




 




The protesters’ grievances were centred on the 2024 collapse of a roof at the newly renovated 

Novi Sad train station

 in northern Serbia, which killed 16 people. Allegations of state involvement through corruption in the procurement process and lowered building standards have been denied by the government. But they nonetheless sparked large nationwide protests.




 




Focus group participants expressed anger and underlying fear about harassment during the protests by what they said were government-funded gangs. They also spoke of their concern at the threats and violence directed towards them, not only as they protested but also when walking in areas near government buildings in main cities. Several students reported feeling threatened even in their own homes.




 




At the same time, the students voiced dissatisfaction with teachers who were not supportive of their movement, and other students who opposed them. This dissatisfaction extended to older family members and relatives who repeated government-controlled media fabrications about the protests. These included claims that the students were being paid by foreign anti-Serbian groups.




 




Despite the fear of arrest or worse, and despondency that change could really occur, the students who took part in the focus groups were resilient. They were focused on their long-term goal of regime change, with many students talking with pride about creating a leaderless movement that was organising candidates to challenge Vučić in an election.




 




Several participants reported feeling spontaneous, intense experiences of national pride when taking part in the protests. Some spoke of taking back national symbols such as the Serbian flag to counter propaganda that they were not patriotic and wanted to destroy the country.




 




Feelings of solidarity 

were also experienced

 when minority Bosniak Muslim students from Novi Pazar University in south-western Serbia joined the protests. As one participant said:




 




They’re a minority which was at odds with Serbia, with Serbian nationals actually. So now we had that part of reunification with them and they’re a Muslim minority. They are really active in these protests and student protests and it’s been wonderful.




 




Another member of the focus group noted that they expected elections to be “brutal”. But they were optimistic about the prospect of unseating the Vučić government. They said: “I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”




 




At the same time, most of the students did not dare to dream that they would succeed in ousting a government that had held a 12-year grip on power. It is stunning now after Vučić’s concession speech in which he admitted “it is clear that we have lost these elections” to know that they were successful just one year later.




 




What’s next?




 




The remarkable victory of the Student List should give hope to any group opposing a corrupt, authoritarian regime that a core commitment to democracy is precisely what attracts voters to choose progressive change.




 




However, while there will be euphoria, pride and tears of joy in Serbia as the election result sinks in, there may also be groups who are fearful of change and that the new government 

may seek accountability

 for members of the ousted regime. Some theorists of political emotions talk about the 

possibility for revenge

 to be enacted by winners, especially when a fight for power has been bitter.




 




For those on the losing side, meanwhile, electoral defeat 

can bring grief

, anxiety and anger. But acknowledging these emotions and coming to terms with loss can bring openness to change. In his concession speech, 

Vučić said

: “I do not want unrest, I do not want killings, I do not want anything like that on the streets.”




 




The Student List’s commitment to democracy, pluralism and justice should also override any desire for redress. The movement has 

actively avoided developing

 a victim identity, taking responsibility for enacting change themselves.




 




As one focus group participant said:




Of course, they [the government] are the problem. I’m not trying to deny that. But I would blame us more … because, I mean, we chose them, we keep choosing them. Okay, they do steal when it comes to the elections, they do many things, they hide, they try to control the media and everything. But at the same time, we don’t have the opposition and we have that state of mind that is allowing them to do everything they’re doing.




 




There are various other challenges facing the Student List. These include adapting the movement’s leaderless organisational assemblage into a government capable of delivering the reforms required for EU membership.




 




But regardless of what happens next, it was certainly a privilege to talk to the students at a time when change did not seem possible and to provide encouragement and support when there was little outside recognition of their struggles and sacrifices.







 










Gavin Brent Sullivan

, Professor of Social Psychology, 

International Psychoanalytic University Berlin

 and 

Tereza Capelos

, Professor of Political Psychology, Department of Politics and International Relations, 

University of Southampton
